# GDPR Legal Bases

Under GDPR Art. 6, **no processing is lawful unless it fits one of six named bases**: consent,
contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, or legitimate interests. The requirement
is not "have a good reason" — it is to pick one basis *per purpose*, in advance, and to be able to
name it.

## The mapping in [[privacy-policy-template]]

§5 does exactly that: a purpose column and a basis column, one row per activity.

| Purpose | Basis claimed |
|---|---|
| Operate, maintain and secure the Service | **Legitimate interests** — running a safe, functioning website |
| Respond to emails, questions or feedback | **Consent** / steps taken at your request |
| Comply with legal obligations and lawful requests | **Legal obligation** |
| Detect, prevent and address abuse, fraud or security incidents | **Legitimate interests** |

Three of the six bases used, three unused — contract, vital interests and public task are simply
inapplicable to a static personal site and are not listed. The section closes by ruling out
advertising, profiling and automated decision-making producing legal or similarly significant
effects, which is Art. 22 answered pre-emptively rather than a marketing claim.

## Why the per-purpose granularity matters

A basis is not a property of an organisation, it is a property of a *processing operation*. The
same email address is held under consent when you write in and could be held under legal obligation
if it were subpoenaed — different bases, different rights attached. That is why §9's rights list is
asymmetric: **withdrawal of consent** only bites on the rows where consent is the basis, and
**objection** only bites on the legitimate-interests rows.

Legitimate interests is the only basis here carrying a balancing test — the controller's interest
against the data subject's rights. It passes easily precisely because so little is collected; see
[[data-minimisation]]. The two concepts are load-bearing for each other.

## Beyond Art. 6

The policy pairs the GDPR mapping with a CCPA/CPRA track that works on a different logic entirely —
not "name your basis" but "disclose, and honour opt-outs" — with a no-sale/no-share attestation and
a 45-day response window against GDPR's 30. §9.3 extends a catch-all to LGPD and PIPEDA. The
supervisory authority is named concretely (Poland's UODO), which is the detail most template
policies leave blank.
